title: Borobudur built
hookLine: in Java, a stone mountain of a monument, carved with the life and the Jataka

lines: A HILL OF TERRACES IN JAVA.
NO HALL INSIDE. YOU WALK IT.
cards: From a distance, across the green fields of central Java, in Indonesia, it looks like a hill that someone has tidied.
Gray stone stacked in terraces, narrowing as it rises, with a crown of bell-shaped stupas on top and volcanoes behind it. Walk closer and the stone turns into pictures.

Panel after panel, wall after wall: a prince in a palace, a woman asleep, a forest hermit, a hare by a fire, ships at sea. There is no hall to step into out of the sun. The whole thing is meant to be walked.

teach.h: A STUPA BUILT OVER A HILL.
teach.b: First, the shape. Borobudur is a stupa, the same kind of monument as those at Sanchi and the Shwedagon.

But its builders raised it over a natural hill, wrapping the hill in stone, terrace above terrace, so the stupa became a mountain you can climb. There is no room inside to gather in. The monument itself is the path.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA'S LIFE, PANEL BY PANEL.
teach.b: Second, the life of the Buddha in stone.
Along the walls of one gallery, carved panels tell his story in order: the prince in the palace, the sights that troubled him, leaving home, the years of seeking, the awakening, the first teaching.
Scholars match these panels to a Sanskrit telling of the life called the Lalitavistara.

teach.h: THE JATAKA: LIVES BEFORE THAT LIFE.
teach.b: Third, the lives before that life. Other panels carve the Jataka, the stories of the Buddha's past births as an animal, a king, a merchant, a hermit.
In one, a hare with nothing to offer a hungry traveler but himself leaps into the fire. Stories like these teach the long patience it takes to grow a bodhisattva's heart, one life at a time.

teach.h: A BOOK YOU READ WITH YOUR FEET.
teach.b: Fourth, a book you read with your feet.

The panels run in order around each terrace, so a pilgrim reads them by walking around the monument with it on the right, the way stupas are circled in respect, and climbs a terrace only after finishing the story below.
Nobody hurries Borobudur. You read it slowly or not at all. Tomorrow, the climb itself, all the way to the top.

how: Buddhist pilgrims, especially at the Vesak festival, walk Borobudur's terraces clockwise, keeping the monument on their right, and the carved panels of the Buddha's life and past lives are read in order as they go.

games.q: you're a pilgrim at the foot of Borobudur, and you want to read the stories in the stone. how do you begin?
o: climb straight to the top for the view first.
walk around the first terrace, keeping it on your right.
pick your favorite panel and skip the rest.
games.why: the panels run in order around each terrace. pilgrims circle with the monument on their right and finish a terrace before climbing to the next.

practice: Stand in your mind at the foot of Borobudur in the early light, gray stone rising in steps above you, and let your eyes travel up, terrace by terrace, to the stupas on top.
Then come back down to a single carved panel at eye level and look at it the way you'd look at a picture in a children's book, one figure, one gesture, one moment, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Borobudur built. A stupa raised over a hill in Java, terrace on terrace, carved with the Buddha's life and his past lives, meant to be read by walking. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: a birth story, a tale of one of the Buddha's past lives.

carryVoice: Your line: a mountain of stone. Every terrace holds a chapter of the story. That's day eight hundred ninety.
